This is the geo-referencing pipeline we helped develop.
The pipeline takes as input a CSV file containing
collection site records extracted from EMu.
Site descriptions, which are often provided in narrative form,
are preprocessed using an LLM with geo-names and
Wikidata serving as knowledge bases.

We developed a preprocessing methodology that automatically
populates missing locality fields using information
extracted from the site description.
The workflow, the preprocessing workflow, processes site
records from a CSV file and automatically populates
missing locality fields. It first cleans
and extracts location information,
then uses an LLM to interpret the complete site description and
populate the locality hierarchy.
For fields that remain empty, a per entity fallback uses
spelling correction,
geo names, Wikidata, and the LLM to identify
possible values. Finally, hierarchy enrichment
fills gaps and verifies geographic consistency
before producing the processed CSV with confidence
ratings.

After the preprocessing, we do the georeferencing.
The georeferencing workflow determines the latitude and
longitude values of a collection site using the
available locality information.
It queries geo names, Wikidata, or Wikipedia for
matching geographic entities, starting from the most specific
location and progressing to the least specific.
So from the nearest named place down to the
continent level.
Candidate entities are then scored using multiple evidence
signals, such as name similarity and geographic hierarchy.
The best matching candidate is selected, and its coordinates
are retrieved. If no suitable match is found, the latitude and
longitude are left blank.
Given these sample locality values, our georeferencing method
first searches using the most specific locality, which
in this example is Mount Mozenberg from the nearest named place
field.
Since no match meets the required scoring threshold,
the method proceeds to the next locality level,
Mozenberg, from the township field.
A suitable match is found at this level, and its
corresponding latitude and longitude values are retrieved.
We compared three knowledge bases, geo names, Wikidata,
and Wikipedia. We evaluated the methods using
100 randomly selected site records from the UK data set.
The evaluation data set was manually annotated
using Wikidata, Wikipedia, and Google as
reference sources. Accuracy was measured based on
whether the predicted coordinates were within a 0.1
degrees threshold of the manually identified
coordinates.
We have observed that the three knowledge bases have different
strengths and limitations. Geo names
performs well for administrative and hierarchical place
names but has relatively limited content and a
strict geographic hierarchy.
Wikidata provides
broader coverage, particularly for natural and
general geographic features, although its hierarchy
data can be noisy.
While Wikipedia offers the most comprehensive
information, but searches tend to be noisier
and slower, often returning multiple irrelevant
articles.
